title: Guidelines for Seizure Prophylaxis in Patients with Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Statement for Healthcare Professionals from the Neurocritical Care Society

recommendations.text: Neurocritical Care Society statement built on a systematic review and meta-analysis of antiseizure medication (ASM) prophylaxis in adults with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, graded with GRADE methodology. The initial search yielded 1988 articles, of which 10 formed the basis of the recommendations. The panel states that overall the quality of evidence is low, precluding strong recommendations.

The guideline suggests that either ASM or no ASM may be used in patients hospitalized with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage who have no history of clinical or electrographic seizures (conditional recommendation, low quality of evidence). No significant difference was found in early seizure, adverse events, mortality, or functional outcomes when ASM was compared with no ASM.

If an ASM is used, the guideline suggests either levetiracetam or phenytoin/fosphenytoin (conditional recommendation, very low quality of evidence). Fewer early seizures were observed with phenytoin/fosphenytoin and a lower risk of neurologic decline with levetiracetam, but with low certainty of evidence; mortality did not differ significantly between treatment types.

If an ASM is used, the guideline suggests either a short (<=3 days) or a long (>3 days) duration of prophylaxis (conditional recommendation, moderate quality of evidence). Extended use may be associated with lower seizure risk but at the same time with a higher risk of adverse effects.

Teaching point on where practice outruns evidence: this graded society document does not establish a single default duration of prophylaxis. Its duration comparison is anchored at 3 days, and the panel could not favour a short course over an extended one. Fixed 3-7 day prophylaxis defaults that appear in many local order sets and protocols are therefore a local convention, not a graded recommendation from this guideline. Educational use only; management decisions rest with the treating team.
